# Fix exposure

- Route: `/tools/fix-photo-exposure`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `fix-photo-exposure`

## Summary

Set the exposure in stops, then recover highlights and shadows separately while the histogram shows you what is left to work with. (Photo editing)

## Details

An exposure problem is a histogram problem: the data is piled against the right edge (overexposed) or the left edge (underexposed), and the fix is to move it back toward the middle without throwing away what is still there. In Aperture that takes two layers from the Basic panel. Exposure (EV) shifts everything by whole or fractional stops in linear light, which repositions the pile. The Tone group then works on the ends independently: Highlights and Whites compress or extend the bright side, Shadows and Blacks the dark side, each with a luminance weight so the midtones are barely touched. The live RGB and luma histogram under the panels tells you when the pile has stopped touching the edge, and the press-and-hold compare key tells you whether you have gone too far.
### What it does
- Exposure (EV) from -5 to +5 moves the whole photo by stops in linear light, the same unit as the camera: -1 EV halves the light, which turns a clipped white of 255 into a flat gray of 188 with no detail in it, and turns 230 into 168.
- Highlights from -100 to +100 compresses or opens the tones above a luma of 0.4, reaching full strength at white; -100 brings pure white down to 0.75 and leaves middle gray at 0.48.
- Shadows from -100 to +100 does the same from black up to a luma of 0.6; +100 lifts a 0.05 near-black to 0.295 while 0.5 only moves to 0.519.
- Whites and Blacks are narrower and weaker versions for the last quarter of each end: Whites acts above a luma of 0.75 and Blacks below 0.25, each with a maximum shift of 0.15.
- The histogram shows red, green, blue and luma counts of the current preview, so a single clipped channel (a red flower, a blue sky) is visible even when the overall picture looks fine.
### How to use it
1. Read the histogram: Open the photo and look where the mass sits. A spike at the far right is clipped highlights; a spike at the far left is crushed shadows.
2. Move the exposure: Drag Exposure (EV) in half-stop steps until the midtones look right. Ignore the ends for now; they are the next step.
3. Recover the ends: For an overexposed photo pull Highlights negative and, if the brightest areas are still flat, Whites negative. For an underexposed photo raise Shadows and, if needed, Blacks.
4. Verify and export: Check that the histogram no longer touches an edge, hold the backslash key to compare with the original, and export at full resolution.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- Recovery works on tones the file still holds; 16-bit TIFF sources, opened signed in, keep more highlight gradation than 8-bit JPEGs when pulled down.
- A large negative exposure on a JPEG reveals the compression blocks that were hidden in the bright areas; exporting as JPG at quality 92 or higher avoids adding more.
### Technical details
- Exposure decodes sRGB to linear (v / 12.92 below 0.04045, otherwise ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) to the power 2.4), multiplies by 2 to the power EV, adds Offset, clamps to 0 to 1, re-encodes and applies 1 / Gamma. Clipping is final: a channel that was already 1.0 in the file has no hidden data, so -1 EV turns it into 0.735 (188) flat.
- Tone computes L as the BT.709 luma (0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B) and four weights: Shadows 1 - smoothstep(0, 0.6, L), Highlights smoothstep(0.4, 1, L), Blacks 1 - smoothstep(0, 0.25, L), Whites smoothstep(0.75, 1, L), where smoothstep(a, b, x) is t squared times (3 - 2t) for t = (x - a) / (b - a) clamped.
- The luma change is 0.25 times (shadows / 100) times its weight plus 0.25 times (highlights / 100) times its weight plus 0.15 times (blacks / 100) times its weight plus 0.15 times (whites / 100) times its weight. The clamped new luma divided by the old luma (floored at 0.0001) scales R, G and B together, so Tone never changes hue.
- Weights at a few luma values: at L = 0.1 Shadows is 0.926 and Blacks 0.648; at L = 0.5 Shadows and Highlights are both 0.074; at L = 0.8 Highlights is 0.741 and Whites 0.104; at L = 0.9 Highlights is 0.926 and Whites 0.648.
- The preview is drawn on your GPU (WebGL2) from a 1920 px copy; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same formulas, and the two agree within a small documented tolerance, at most a few 8-bit levels (grain is exact). Exposure and Tone are pure per-pixel math, so they sit at the identical end of that tolerance.
- The histogram is computed from the preview, so it reflects the 1920 px copy; the full-resolution export has the same distribution because the formulas are per pixel and do not depend on the image size.
### When not to use it
If the only problem is a slightly flat or dull photo that is neither too bright nor too dark, this is the wrong page: the contrast tool or a curve will do more with less. If the photo is overexposed to the point that faces or skies are solid white, no slider will bring texture back, because the JPEG never stored it; the Heal tool can patch small blown spots, but a blown sky needs a different photograph. And if the exposure problem is confined to the edges, a vignette at a positive amount is simpler than a masked exposure layer.
### Use cases
- Blown-out beach or snow scene: Exposure -0.7 EV, then Highlights -50 and Whites -20 to bring the sand or snow back from white toward a textured 0.7; the true-white specular points stay white.
- Dark concert or night photo: Exposure +1.5 EV first, then Highlights -40 to protect the stage lights that the exposure pushed to the edge, then Shadows +20 for the crowd.
- Window in the background: Leave the global exposure alone and add a second Exposure layer at -1.5 EV under a linear gradient or brush mask covering only the window.
- Camera metered on the wrong subject: A face that is too dark against a bright wall takes Exposure +0.5 EV with a Select subject mask so the wall does not come along.
### FAQ
Q: Can clipped highlights be recovered from a JPEG?
A: Not if they are truly clipped. A pixel stored as 255, 255, 255 has no information left, and lowering exposure turns it into a flat gray (188 at -1 EV). What usually can be recovered are near-white areas such as 240 to 254, which Highlights -60 compresses to around 205 to 217 with their texture intact. A raw file would hold more, but the editor works on the image the browser can decode.
Q: What order should I apply Exposure and Tone in?
A: Exposure first, Tone above it. Tone weights depend on the luma it receives, so if you recover highlights and then raise exposure, the recovery no longer targets the right pixels. Layers apply bottom to top, and the Basic panel creates them in that order.
Q: What is the difference between Highlights and Whites?
A: Highlights starts at a luma of 0.4 and reaches full strength at 1.0 with a maximum shift of 0.25; Whites starts at 0.75 with a maximum shift of 0.15. Use Highlights for a bright sky or skin, Whites for the last step before pure white when the brightest tones still look flat.
Q: Why does -1 EV not simply halve the pixel values?
A: Because the halving happens in linear light and the file is sRGB-encoded. A mid gray of 128 becomes 92, not 64, and a bright 230 becomes 168. The sRGB curve compresses light tones, so a one-stop change looks smaller in the top half of the range than in the bottom.
Q: How is this different from an automatic exposure fix?
A: The Auto look in the Presets panel adds a reasonable starting stack, and you can undo it with one step. The sliders on this page are the manual version, with the histogram and a compare key, for photos where an automatic guess gets the subject wrong.
Q: Does fixing exposure change the colors of the photo?
A: Exposure scales all three channels equally in linear light, and Tone scales them equally by a luma ratio, so hue is preserved until a channel clips. A sunset that loses its red when you raise exposure has a clipped red channel, which the RGB histogram will show as a red spike at the right edge.
